name: TRT / testosterone for jaw

card.summary: The idea of using testosterone or related androgens to masculinise the jaw and face; testosterone therapy is established for low testosterone, but no study tests it for jaw structure.
card.aka: DHT for jaw, hormones for masculinization
card.note: Testosterone is a controlled, prescription-only drug in many countries; adverse effects and fertility suppression are documented.

quick.overview:
Some looksmaxxing discussion holds that testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), or related androgens such as DHT, can masculinise the face and jaw. Testosterone medication is approved for men with low natural testosterone, for masculinising therapy in transgender men and for some other uses.

The sources reviewed give no study of testosterone for jaw or facial bone structure in the context of appearance enhancement. Medical descriptions cover hypogonadism, side effects and legal status.
quick.mechanism: Testosterone acts on the androgen receptor and is converted in tissues to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-alpha-reductase. DHT is associated with facial and body hair growth and male genital development. Testosterone is linked to musculoskeletal development, voice deepening and libido.
quick.risks: Reported effects of testosterone medication include acne, oily skin, hair loss, breast enlargement in men, raised red blood cell count, worsened sleep apnoea, liver toxicity with some forms and suppression of sperm production. Testosterone is Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU.

lead: TRT or testosterone for jaw refers to the belief, discussed in looksmaxxing communities, that testosterone replacement or related androgens such as DHT can masculinise the jaw and other facial structure. Testosterone medication is used to treat males with low or absent natural production, for masculinising hormone therapy and for certain breast cancers.[1]

Testosterone is a controlled substance in many places, and it can suppress sperm production, cause acne, hair loss and breast enlargement in men and raise haematocrit.[1] DHT is a testosterone metabolite made by 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues and is linked to facial and body hair growth.[2] No studies were found on testosterone therapy for jaw structure.

paras: The concept connects testosterone, and in some versions DHT, to the development of masculine facial features. Testosterone medication is available as injections, gels, patches, oral, buccal, nasal and implant forms.[1]

Evidence for treating low testosterone from ageing alone is described as unclear. The FDA stated in 2015 that neither benefit nor safety was established, while a 2020 American College of Physicians guideline supports discussing treatment for men with age-related low testosterone and sexual dysfunction.[1]

DHT is made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase. Studies of people with 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency indicate DHT's role in male genital development, while affected people still develop several male secondary characteristics at puberty, such as voice deepening and musculoskeletal development, with reduced facial and body hair.[2]

Reported effects include acne, oily skin, swelling, hair loss, breast enlargement in men, raised haematocrit, worsened sleep apnoea, liver toxicity and mood or behavioural changes. Exogenous testosterone can suppress sperm production, sometimes reversibly. Cardiovascular risk is debated, and in February 2025 the FDA removed cardiovascular language from the boxed warning and added a blood pressure warning. Testosterone is contraindicated in prostate cancer and in pregnancy.[1]
Anabolic-androgenic steroids can prematurely close growth plates in adolescents.[3]

Testosterone is Schedule III in the United States, Schedule IV in Canada, Class C in the United Kingdom and prescription-only in the EU. It is banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[1]
